E2.question: What evidence is relevant to understanding how Campus belonging (item 1) (belong1) can contribute to an elevated screening-model prediction in college students, without treating it as a causal diagnosis?
E2.answer: Evidence suggests that social support is a significant statistical contributor to positive mental health outcomes in college students. Specifically, high levels of social support have been associated with reduced levels of depression and anxiety, as well as enhanced life satisfaction and subjective well-being. Furthermore, research indicates that students who report average to high levels of well-being tend to experience better current and long-term outcomes, including academic success. These findings suggest that strong social support and belonging may act as protective factors, statistically correlating with lower levels of distress and better overall mental health outcomes.

E4.question: What evidence is relevant to understanding how Public institution (inst_public) may appear among model contributors for student mental-health screening support?
E4.answer: The evidence suggests that public institutions, such as identified public college health centers, are relevant contributors because they are primary sites for mental health screening efforts. These settings may need to implement structured screening, such as using the PHQ-2, because a complaint-based approach can fail to detect depression if patients mask symptoms or report somatic complaints to avoid stigma. Furthermore, the necessity of screening is supported by the high prevalence of depression among college students and the need to improve early identification. Public institutions are also involved in universal school screening, which aims to connect students and families to cost-effective community and school mental health services.

E5.question: What evidence discusses protective or lower-risk factors relevant to Academic impairment, Age, Loneliness in college student mental-health screening contexts?
E5.answer: Evidence suggests that high levels of social support are a significant protective factor, as research indicates that social support mitigates mental health challenges and is associated with reduced levels of depression and anxiety among college students. Furthermore, experiencing average to high levels of well-being is linked to better current and long-term outcomes, including academic success, regardless of reported psychological distress. While the term "loneliness" is not used, the importance of social connectedness is noted as a key outcome affected by mental health. Regarding academic impairment, mental health status affects important outcomes such as academic performance and academic retention. Screening efforts may also identify students who experience poor academic progress as part of a broader risk assessment.

This context sheds light on why one in four incoming freshman college students leave within one year of arriving on campus [8], with a similar proportion diagnosed or treated for depression and anxiety annually [9]. These disturbing trends existed before 2020 but were exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. A meta-analysis found that 31% of college students worldwide reported symptoms of anxiety and 34% reported symptoms of depression during the early stages of the pandemic [10]. Rates varied between countries (partly due to methodo- logical differences), but American college students reported the highest rates of both anxiety (52%) and depression (69%). At one university in the United States, 18% of students had sui- cidal thoughts [11]. In studies that disaggregated data by gender, males were somewhat more likely than females to report symptoms of anxiety (36% compared to 30%), while females were much more likely than males to report symptoms of depression (56% compared to 34%). More recent research provides strong evidence for higher rates of both anxiety and depression among female college students compared to males [12–14]. A substantial body of research, dating back more than a century to Durkheim’s ground- breaking work on factors contributing to suicide, has shown that mental health challenges are mitigated by social support [15–17]. Among college students, high levels of social support are associated with reduced levels of depression and anxiety [18, 19], lower suicide risk [17], and enhanced life satisfaction and subjective well-being [20, 21]. Available Knowledge/Review of the Literature According to the U.S. Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF), depression is among the leading causes of disability in individuals 15 years of age and older (Siu & U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), 2016). By 2020, depressive disorders are predicted to be the second leading cause of disability and death (Soltani, Smith, Beck, & Johnson, 2014). Prevalence of depression among college students accounts for approximately 16.7% and is more than twice as common among college students compared to the general population (Liu et al., 2019; English & Campbell, 2019). Thus, depression is highly prevalent and appears to be increasing. Depression is one of the leading health concerns in college population, yet roughly half of college students with depression receive treatment (English & Campbell, 2019). Mental health among college students affects important outcomes such as social connectedness, academic performance, academic retention, and future economic productivity, which should be a significant concern for certain stakeholders such as campus administrators, college professors, and parents (Lipson, Gaddis, Heinze, & Eisenberg, 2015; Ebert et al., 2018). In addition, depression has been associated with increased health care costs such as emergency department visits and inpatient hospitalizations (Wright et al., 2015). Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified.
